messages.content: What is clock gating?

CONCEPT:
Clock gating disables the clock signal to inactive logic blocks.

WHY IT MATTERS:
It reduces unnecessary switching activity and therefore lowers dynamic power.

EXAMPLE:
An idle GPU compute unit can have its clock gated until new work arrives.
What is power gating?

CONCEPT:
Power gating disconnects an inactive circuit block from its power supply using sleep transistors.

WHY IT MATTERS:
It reduces leakage power when a block is not being used.

EXAMPLE:
A processor may power gate an unused accelerator block during a long idle period.
What is dynamic power?

CONCEPT:
Dynamic power is power consumed when circuit nodes switch between logic states.

WHY IT MATTERS:
It increases with switching activity, capacitance, clock frequency, and approximately the square of supply voltage.

EXAMPLE:
Increasing a GPU clock frequency while keeping activity constant generally increases dynamic power.
What is leakage power?

CONCEPT:
Leakage power is power consumed by transistor leakage currents even when useful switching is not occurring.

WHY IT MATTERS:
It contributes to static power and becomes important in advanced semiconductor processes.

EXAMPLE:
A powered but idle CPU core can still consume energy because transistors leak current.
What is DVFS?

CONCEPT:
Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling changes operating voltage and frequency according to performance demand.

WHY IT MATTERS:
It trades performance against power and energy consumption.

EXAMPLE:
A processor can reduce both voltage and clock frequency during a light workload to save power.
What is IR drop?

CONCEPT:
IR drop is the reduction in supply voltage caused by current flowing through resistive power-delivery paths.

WHY IT MATTERS:
Excessive voltage drop can reduce timing margin and cause unreliable circuit operation.

EXAMPLE:
A highly active GPU region can draw enough current to lower the local supply voltage seen by nearby logic.
What is a cache?

CONCEPT:
A cache is a small, fast memory that stores frequently or recently accessed data close to the processor.

WHY IT MATTERS:
It reduces the average latency and bandwidth cost of accessing slower memory levels.

EXAMPLE:
A CPU may find frequently reused data in its L1 cache instead of fetching it from DRAM.
What is HBM?

CONCEPT:
High Bandwidth Memory is stacked DRAM connected through a very wide memory interface.

WHY IT MATTERS:
It provides much higher memory bandwidth than conventional off-package memory interfaces while keeping the memory physically close to the compute device.

EXAMPLE:
AI accelerators use HBM to feed large amounts of model and activation data to highly parallel compute units.
What is quantization?

CONCEPT:
Quantization represents model values using lower-precision numerical formats.

WHY IT MATTERS:
It can reduce model memory usage and computational cost, often improving inference efficiency.

EXAMPLE:
An inference model may use 4-bit weights instead of 16-bit weights to reduce the amount of memory required.
What is an embedding?

CONCEPT:
An embedding is a numerical vector representation of data such as text.

WHY IT MATTERS:
Items with similar meaning can be represented near one another in vector space, enabling semantic comparison and retrieval.

EXAMPLE:
A RAG system can compare a question embedding against PDF chunk embeddings to retrieve relevant passages.
